title: Rewrite bad tickets: a graded bank of 12
summary: Twelve weak tickets to rewrite, in three sets: bug reports, requests, and mixed or internal tickets. Each has a model rewrite and a rubric to mark yourself against.

lessons.title: Set A: rewrite four vague bug reports
lessons.body:
A weak bug report makes the developer ask questions before they can start. Your rewrite should let them start without a call. Use this skeleton from earlier units:

```text
Title: [Where] [what is wrong] [for whom/when]
Environment: app/web, version, browser/device, account role
Steps to reproduce: 1... 2... 3...
Expected: ...
Actual: ...
Frequency / scope: always, sometimes, how many customers
Evidence: screenshot, shift id, time, log
Impact + workaround: ...
```

**Method for a rewrite when you do not have the facts.** You often cannot invent details. Rewrite with what is given, mark unknowns as **'to confirm'**, and add the questions you would ask the reporter. In this bank, fill plausible details from the dispatch product and mark them as assumed. In real life you would ask first.

**Worked example.**

Bad: 'Schedule wrong. Please fix.'

Rewritten:

```text
Title: Schedule view shows pharmacist shift one hour late for Arizona pharmacists
Environment: web app 2.3.2, Chrome, dispatcher role
Steps: 1. Open Schedule for week of 10 Nov. 2. Find shift 8812 (Mesa Care, Arizona pharmacist). 3. Compare start time with the mobile app.
Expected: 09:00 in both.
Actual: web shows 10:00, mobile shows 09:00.
Scope: all Arizona shifts seen so far (6); other regions fine.
Impact: dispatchers misread arrival times. Workaround: check mobile app.
To confirm: does this happen only since the 2.3.2 release?
```

Checks for marking yourself: (1) the title carries where, what and who; (2) steps could be followed by a stranger; (3) expected and actual are separate; (4) scope and workaround are stated; (5) unknowns are labelled, not hidden.

Do the four exercises below and compare. A rewrite does not need to match word for word. It has to pass the rubric.
keyPoints: A rewrite must let the developer start without a call.
Separate expected from actual, and give steps a stranger could follow.
Mark unknown details 'to confirm' and list the questions you would ask.
Title should say where, what and for whom.
lessons.interviewAngle: Practical tests often hand you a bad ticket and ask for a rewrite. Narrate the method: title, environment, steps, expected, actual, scope, impact, unknowns. State that you would normally ask the reporter for missing facts. Keep the rewrite short and point to the one assumption you would check first.

exercises.prompt: A ticket says 'Notifications broken'. What is the best first improvement to the title?
choices: Say which notification, for whom, and what is wrong: 'SMS not sent when shift is filled for Pharmacy 12'
exercises.explanation: A specific title tells triage and developers what and where, which urgency words do not.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite (1/4): 'App broken pls fix asap!!!'. Assume details where needed, marking them as assumed, and add the questions you would ask.
exercises.answer:
**Title:** Dispatcher web app shows error when assigning a pharmacist to a shift (assumed)
**Environment:** web 2.3.2, Chrome, dispatcher role (to confirm)
**Steps:** 1. Open an open shift. 2. Choose a pharmacist. 3. Click Assign.
**Expected:** Shift becomes Assigned. **Actual:** error banner 'Something went wrong' (to confirm exact text).
**Scope:** to confirm: one user or all? **Impact:** cannot fill shifts; workaround to confirm.
**Questions for reporter:** What were you doing? What does the screen say? Since when? Does it happen for others? Can you send a screenshot and the time?

**Title:** Shift-filled text message not received by pharmacy contacts since Monday (assumed)
**Environment:** production, SMS channel, all pharmacies or Pharmacy 12 (to confirm)
**Steps:** 1. Create a test shift for Pharmacy 12. 2. Assign a pharmacist. 3. Watch for the text to the pharmacy contact.
**Expected:** text within 1 minute. **Actual:** none arrives; email arrives normally.
**Scope:** to confirm number of pharmacies. **Severity:** Major if all, because staff cannot confirm fills. **Evidence:** shift ids and send times to attach.
**Questions:** Which notification? Which pharmacies? Since when? Any phone number changes?

**Title:** Shift start time in the pharmacist mobile app differs from the dispatcher web view by one hour (assumed)
**Steps:** 1. Open shift 8812 in the web Schedule. 2. Open the same shift in the mobile app signed in as the assigned pharmacist.
**Expected:** same time in both. **Actual:** web 10:00, mobile 09:00 (assumed).
**To confirm:** which screen is wrong, time zone of the pharmacy and pharmacist, version, whether it began after a release.
**Impact:** pharmacists could arrive an hour early or late. **Workaround:** state time in the confirmation message.
rubric: Says which time is wrong and where

exercises.prompt: Rewrite (4/4): 'Cant login.' Use an Access-type ticket and include what support should check before escalating.
exercises.answer:
**Title:** New dispatcher cannot log in; 'Invalid credentials' after password reset (assumed)
**Who:** user name, pharmacy, role, when the account was created (to confirm)
**Steps tried:** reset email requested at 09:10; link used at 09:15; new password rejected.
**Expected:** login succeeds. **Actual:** invalid credentials banner. **Browser:** Chrome (to confirm).
**Support checks first:** account exists and is active; email address correct; reset email not in spam; user is on the correct site; try another browser; check if only this user is affected.
**Escalate if:** the account is active and the reset still fails, with the account id and times.
rubric: Who is affected and what was tried

lessons.title: Set B: rewrite four vague requests
lessons.body:
A feature request is a wish until you find the problem behind it. A good rewrite keeps the customer's goal, drops the proposed solution, and makes it testable. The skeleton:

```text
Title: [User] can [do something] [so that outcome]
Background: who asked, how often, what they do today
Story: As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]
Acceptance criteria (Given/When/Then or checklist)
Out of scope
Open questions
```

**Method.** Ask 'what are you trying to get done?' until you hear the underlying need. 'Make it faster' might mean the schedule loads slowly with 500 shifts, or that filling an urgent shift takes too many clicks. Those are different tickets. Quantify: 'loads in under 3 seconds with 500 shifts' can be tested, 'faster' cannot.

**Worked example.**

Bad: 'Need export.'

Rewritten:

```text
Title: Dispatcher can export monthly assignments to CSV so billing can reconcile them
Background: Mesa Care exports by copying the screen; about 90 rows a month.
Story: As a dispatcher I want to export a month of assignments, so that finance can reconcile them without retyping.
Acceptance criteria:
- Given a month with assignments, when I choose Export, then a CSV downloads within 10 seconds.
- Columns: pharmacy, pharmacist, shift start, status.
- Only assignments the user is allowed to see are included.
- An empty month gives a clear message, not an empty file.
Out of scope: PDF, scheduled exports
Questions: Which columns does finance need? Date format?
```

Marking checklist: user and benefit clear, solution not assumed, criteria testable and measurable, edge cases (empty, permission), out of scope stated, questions listed.

A ticket that asks for a solution ('add a button') should become a ticket about the problem; the button may be the answer or not.
keyPoints: Find the goal behind the request and drop the proposed solution.
Replace words like faster or better with a measurable criterion.
Write testable acceptance criteria including empty and permission cases.
State what is out of scope and what is still unknown.
lessons.interviewAngle: This is the BA and product-owner heart of your resume: you turned customer feedback into stories with acceptance criteria. Use one real example, such as the SOS alert feature you scoped, and walk through the question that found the real need.

choices: The schedule loads within 3 seconds with 500 shifts on a standard connection
exercises.explanation: A number and a condition let anyone decide pass or fail. The others are opinions.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite (5/8): 'Need export.' Support heard it from a pharmacy manager who wants to know who accepted each shift request. Write the story and criteria.
exercises.answer:
**Title:** Pharmacy manager can see and export who accepted each shift request so they can confirm coverage
**Story:** As a pharmacy manager I want to list pharmacists who accepted my shift requests, so that I can confirm coverage without calling support.
**Acceptance criteria:** (1) Given requests exist, when I open Requests, then each shows status and the accepting pharmacist. (2) I can export the list to CSV. (3) I only see my pharmacy's data. (4) Requests with no acceptance show 'No pharmacist yet'.
**Out of scope:** notifications about acceptances.
**Questions:** time range needed? Is acceptance time required?
rubric: Testable criteria incl. permission and empty case

exercises.prompt: Rewrite (6/8): 'Make it faster.' Assume a dispatcher complained that filling an urgent shift takes too long.
exercises.answer:
**Title:** Dispatcher can fill an urgent shift in three steps or fewer
**Background:** dispatchers report it takes about eight clicks across three screens to assign a pharmacist to an emergency shift (to confirm by observing).
**Story:** As a dispatcher I want to assign a pharmacist directly from the emergency shift list, so that urgent shifts are filled quickly.
**Acceptance criteria:** assignment possible from the list without opening another page; median time from opening the list to assignment under 30 seconds in a usability test with 3 dispatchers; existing assignment rules still apply.
**Out of scope:** automatic assignment.
**Questions:** Is speed about clicks or about load time?
rubric: Notes the question about the cause

exercises.prompt: Rewrite (7/8): 'Add SMS.' (Context: pharmacists currently get email alerts only.)
exercises.answer:
**Title:** Pharmacists receive emergency shift alerts by SMS as well as email
**Story:** As a pharmacist I want an SMS when a nearby emergency shift appears, so that I see it quickly when I am not at my email.
**Acceptance criteria:** SMS sent within 1 minute of the shift being flagged; only to opted-in pharmacists within the set distance; includes pharmacy name, start time and link; no duplicate texts; opt-out reply stops messages.
**Out of scope:** two-way chat.
**Questions:** Opt-in wording? Cost per message and a monthly cap? Quiet hours?
rubric: Criteria include timing, scope, content and duplicates
Open questions on cost or limits

exercises.answer:
**Title:** Dispatchers can see the monthly shift fill rate by pharmacy
**Background:** managers ask for fill rate each month and currently request it from support, who calculate it with SQL (to confirm).
**Story:** As a dispatcher I want a report of shifts requested, filled and cancelled per pharmacy per month, so that I can see where coverage fails.
**Acceptance criteria:** month and pharmacy filters; shows requested, filled, cancelled and fill rate (filled divided by requested); numbers match the database totals; exports to CSV.
**Out of scope:** charts.
**Questions:** Do cancelled shifts count in the denominator? Who may see which pharmacies?

lessons.title: Set C: rewrite four mixed and internal tickets
lessons.body:
Some bad tickets are not vague bugs or wishes. They bundle three problems, point to a meeting nobody can see, describe a person instead of a problem, or report a failed test without evidence. Fix the structure first, then the content.

**Pattern 1: the bundle.** One ticket contains several unrelated asks. Split it into one ticket per problem, and link them. A bundle cannot be closed cleanly: if two are fixed and one is not, what is its status?

**Pattern 2: the pointer.** 'Fix the thing we discussed' only works for the people in the room. A ticket must stand alone six months later. Write down the decision, the reason and the owner.

**Pattern 3: the complaint.** 'Customer angry' is a feeling. Find the event behind it, the impact in numbers, and what the customer actually needs, then record the customer's exact words in a quote so nothing is lost.

**Pattern 4: the bare test failure.** 'Test failed' needs the test case id, steps, expected, actual, build, environment and evidence, as in your Azure DevOps Test Plans work.

**Worked example (bundle).**

Bad: 'Fix schedule problems: wrong time, cannot export, and new users missing.'

Rewritten as three linked tickets:

```text
DISP-601 Bug: Arizona shifts show one hour off in the web schedule
DISP-602 Request: Export monthly assignments to CSV
DISP-603 Bug: Newly created dispatchers are missing from the user list until next day
Parent / epic: Schedule feedback from Mesa Care call, 10 Nov
```

Each has its own owner, severity and status. The original ticket becomes the parent or is closed with links.

**Checks for marking yourself:** one problem per ticket; standalone description; facts rather than feelings; evidence and identifiers present; next step and owner named.

The four exercises ask for these patterns. Keep your rewrites short: if a section would only say 'none', leave it out.
keyPoints: Split a bundle into linked tickets with their own owners and statuses.
A ticket must make sense without the meeting that created it.
Replace feelings with events, numbers and the customer's exact words.
A failed test needs case id, steps, expected, actual, build and evidence.
lessons.interviewAngle: Use the bundle and meeting-pointer examples when asked how you keep a backlog clean. You wrote tickets from customer calls: say how you captured decisions and owners so nothing lived only in someone's memory. Offer to split any bundle live in the interview, because it is quick and shows judgement.

exercises.prompt: One ticket asks for a bug fix, a new report and a permissions change. What do you do?
choices: Leave it as one ticket for convenience
Split it into linked tickets, one per problem, each with an owner
Close it and ask them to email
exercises.explanation: Separate tickets can be prioritised, assigned and closed independently.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite (9/12): 'Fix the thing from the meeting.' You attended: the team agreed that cancelled shifts should free the pharmacist's calendar slot immediately, which does not happen now. Owner: Priya (dev). Customer: Mesa Care.
exercises.answer:
**Title:** Cancelled shifts do not release the pharmacist's calendar slot
**Background:** Agreed in the 10 Nov call with Mesa Care: when a shift is cancelled, the pharmacist's slot should free immediately. Today it stays blocked until the nightly job.
**Expected:** slot free within 1 minute of cancellation. **Actual:** blocked until about 02:00.
**Acceptance criteria:** cancelling a shift frees the slot immediately for all three cancel reasons; the pharmacist can be assigned elsewhere straight away.
**Owner:** Priya. **Customer to update:** Dana at Mesa Care.
**Decision record:** agreed by product and support on 10 Nov.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite (10/12): 'Customer angry about shifts.' Details you can assume: two emergency shifts at Riverside Pharmacy stayed unfilled last Thursday, and the manager said 'You are costing me money'.
exercises.answer:
**Title:** Two emergency shifts unfilled at Riverside Pharmacy on Thursday 5 Nov: customer escalation
**Facts:** shifts 9021 and 9034 (requested 07:10 and 07:40) stayed open until cancelled at 12:00; alerts were not logged as sent (to confirm).
**Impact:** pharmacy ran short-staffed; manager says the cost to them is significant (quote: 'You are costing me money').
**Needs:** an explanation, a fix date, and assurance for next week.
**Actions:** investigate alert log (Tier 2), call customer today (support lead), link any alert ticket.
**Severity:** Major pending the cause. **Next update to customer:** today by 17:00.
rubric: Replaces anger with events and ids

exercises.prompt: Rewrite (11/12): a QA note that says 'Test failed.' The case was TC-212, 'Assign pharmacist to emergency shift', run on build 2.3.3 in staging, and the shift stayed Open.
exercises.answer:
**Title:** TC-212 fails on build 2.3.3: assigning a pharmacist to an emergency shift leaves the shift Open
**Environment:** staging, build 2.3.3, Chrome, dispatcher role.
**Steps:** 1. Create an emergency shift for Pharmacy 12. 2. Select pharmacist 18 and click Assign. 3. Refresh the shift.
**Expected:** status Assigned and one assignment row. **Actual:** status stays Open; an assignment row appears (id to attach).
**Evidence:** screenshot, request log time 10:42.
**Frequency:** 3 of 3 runs. **Regression?** passed on 2.3.2.
**Linked:** TC-212; story DISP-388.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite (12/12): split this bundle into tickets. 'Pharmacies say shifts show wrong time, can't download assignments, support has no way to see who got alerts, and the login page has a typo.' Give each ticket a title, type and suggested severity or priority.
exercises.answer:
1. **Bug:** Arizona shifts display one hour off in the web schedule. Severity Moderate to Major, priority P2 (wrong times affect arrivals).
2. **Feature request:** Export monthly assignments to CSV. Priority P3, backlog and ranked.
3. **Feature request / internal tool:** Support can view the list of pharmacists who were alerted for a shift. Priority P3; link to alert epic.
4. **Bug (cosmetic):** Typo on the login page. Severity Minor, P4; quick fix, batch with the next release.
All four are linked to a parent 'Feedback from pharmacies, November'.
